topics.title: Critical Comprehension & Literal Extraction
topics.summary: This topic trains you to find, isolate and pick out facts that the author states directly in a passage, without adding your own opinion or outside knowledge.
topics.exam_tip: JAMB often hides literal answers right after transition words like however, indeed, in fact and notably. When a question asks about a detail, find the keyword in the passage and read the sentences just after these words.
topics.analogy: Literal extraction is like a passport control checkpoint. The officer does not care about your feelings; they only check the hard facts printed on the page. If the data does not match the text exactly, entry is denied.

sub_topics.title: Finding Facts and Rhetorical Strategies
sub_topics.note: Literal extraction means finding facts that the author states directly. JAMB uses long sentences, appositives and bracketed statements to bury these facts. Authors use four main styles: Description (painting scenes with sensory details), Narration (telling events in time order), Exposition (explaining step by step and objectively) and Argumentation (using evidence and appeals to persuade). To extract information correctly, separate the main clause from the dependent clauses and modifiers around it.
sub_topics.formula: Correct Literal Option = Textual Fact Paraphrased (Same Meaning)

sub_topics.title: Spotting Distractors and Absolute Words
sub_topics.note: JAMB distractors twist facts by swapping modifiers or by using absolute words such as always, never or solely when the text uses softer words like often, sometimes or generally. An option that cannot be proven by pointing to a sentence in the passage is wrong, even if it is true in real life.
sub_topics.formula: Bait Distractor = Textual Fact + Absolute Modifier (Always / Never / Only)

flashcards.back: Retrieving explicitly stated facts from the text without adding personal interpretation or outside knowledge.
A piece of writing designed entirely to inform, explain, analyze, or illustrate a specific topic objectively.
A rhetorical style that uses logic, evidence, and reasoning to convince the reader of a specific viewpoint.
A chronological sequence of events structured around characters, a setting, a central conflict, and a resolution.
Writing that relies on sensory details and vivid imagery to illustrate a person, place, or object.
Distractors that insert words like always, only, or never into a fact that the text qualified with sometimes or mostly.
Moving your eyes rapidly over a text to locate specific keywords, numbers, names, or phrases.
Reading a passage quickly to understand its general layout, core theme, or main ideas.
Options that change the literal words of the text using synonyms but keep the exact same underlying meaning.
Words that limit a statement (e.g., frequently, rarely, possibly) which must be matched exactly in the correct option.
A noun phrase placed next to another to define it; JAMB uses this to confuse readers about who performed an action.
Information set off by dashes or brackets that can be skipped over to find the main fact.
If an option cannot be proven by pointing to a specific sentence in the text, it is incorrect.
A question asked for dramatic effect rather than to get an answer, highlighting a core point.
When an author uses flashbacks, disrupting the time order to confuse readers about the sequence of events.
Pronouns like it, they, which that require looking back to the previous sentence to find the true noun.
Options that are factually true in real life but are completely missing from the passage; these are incorrect.
The foundation on which the author builds their entire argument.
Semicolons used to link two opposing facts; the correct answer often hinges on this contrast.
Verifying an option word-for-word against the text while scanning for hidden negative words.

topics.title: Deep Inferential Reading & Authorial Intent
topics.summary: This topic trains you to read between the lines: finding meanings that are hinted at but not stated, and decoding the author's tone, mood and purpose.
topics.exam_tip: When a question asks 'What is the attitude of the author?' or 'It can be inferred that...', look closely at the adjectives and adverbs. If an author calls a policy 'a short-sighted gamble', the tone is critical, and the correct answer must show that disapproval.
topics.analogy: Inference is like seeing wet umbrellas walk into a windowless building. Nobody says 'it is raining outside', but the wet umbrellas are clear clues that tell you the weather.

sub_topics.title: Tone, Mood and Intent
sub_topics.note: Inference means reading between the lines to find meanings that are implied but not stated. JAMB tests tone (the writer's attitude, such as cynical, optimistic, patronizing or satirical), mood (the feeling created for the reader) and intent (the writer's purpose, such as to lampoon, to advocate or to demystify). Look for loaded words, emotional adjectives and patterns in punctuation.
sub_topics.formula: Valid Inference = Explicit Textual Clues + Deductive Logic

sub_topics.title: Valid and Invalid Inferences
sub_topics.note: An inference is valid only if it is a direct logical extension of the facts in the text. Anything that goes beyond the clues in the passage is speculation and must be rejected, even when it sounds believable in real life.
sub_topics.formula: Invalid Inference = Speculation Outside the Text

flashcards.back: Drawing logical conclusions from implicit clues and evidence left by the author.
The writer's attitude toward the subject, expressed through word choice and style.
The atmosphere or emotional state created in the reader by the author's words.
Using humor, irony, exaggeration, or ridicule to expose and criticize human flaws or vices.
An attitude marked by a general distrust of human nature, motives, or institutions.
Unbiased, neutral writing that relies on verifiable facts rather than personal feelings.
The main reason an author writes a text (e.g., to persuade, entertain, inform, or criticize).
Information that is hinted at or suggested without being stated directly.
A condescending style that treats the reader or subject with an air of superior intelligence.
A sentimental longing for a past period, event, or condition.
Spotting a contrast between expectation and reality, or between what is said and what is meant.
An incorrect option that turns a specific implicit point into a sweeping universal claim.
Identifying unreasoned judgment or prejudice in the author's choice of words.
Looking at the underlying themes or meanings that run beneath the surface of the text.
Using sharp, ironic language designed to mock, insult, or cause hurt.
A writing style intended to teach, lecture, or moralize.
Replacing a harsh or blunt expression with a milder, indirect one to soften a statement.
A step-by-step process of reasoning where a conclusion follows necessarily from the stated premises.
An outlook influenced by personal opinions, beliefs, and emotional preferences.
An option that sounds plausible in real life but goes far beyond the clues provided in the passage.

topics.title: Figurative Language & Rhetorical Devices
topics.summary: This topic covers the figures of speech JAMB puts in passages, such as metaphor, simile, personification, hyperbole, oxymoron, paradox and irony, and how to explain them in context.
topics.exam_tip: When JAMB asks the meaning of a phrase like 'He was a lion in the academic arena', pick the option that explains the figurative meaning (courage or dominant intelligence), not the literal meaning (animals or physical fighting).
topics.analogy: Figurative language is like a Snapchat filter on plain text. It changes how the text looks and adds style, but the real message underneath stays the same. Look past the filter to see the true message.

sub_topics.title: Common Figures of Speech
sub_topics.note: The most tested figures are: metaphor (direct comparison), simile (comparison using like or as), personification (giving human traits to non-human things), hyperbole (extreme exaggeration), oxymoron (placing contradictory words side by side), paradox (a statement that seems to contradict itself but reveals a deeper truth) and irony (situational, verbal or dramatic contrast). Knowing them stops you from reading figurative expressions literally, which is a common JAMB trap.
sub_topics.formula: Oxymoron = Adjective (Opposite A) + Noun (Opposite B), e.g. deafening silence

sub_topics.title: Paradox and Interpreting Figures in Context
sub_topics.note: A paradox is a statement that looks self-contradictory on the surface but holds a true idea underneath. When a question asks about a figure of speech in a passage, first name the device, then explain what it means in that context.
sub_topics.formula: Paradox = Statement A (True) <-> Statement B (Seems to contradict A but reveals truth)

flashcards.back: A direct comparison between two unrelated things without using comparison words like like or as.
Explicitly comparing two different things using connection words, specifically like or as.
Giving human qualities, emotions, or actions to non-human objects, animals, or abstract ideas.
Deliberate, extreme exaggeration used for emphasis or dramatic effect, not to be taken literally.
Placing two contradictory or opposite terms right next to each other for structural impact.
A statement that appears self-contradictory on the surface but contains an underlying truth.
When a speaker says the exact opposite of what they mean, often with a sarcastic edge.
An event or outcome that turns out to be the direct opposite of what was reasonably expected.
A figure of speech where a part is used to represent the whole, or the whole represents a part.
Replacing the name of an object or concept with something closely associated with it.
An understatement produced by denying the opposite of a statement, often using a double negative.
Words that imitate the natural sound associated with the action or object they describe.
Repeating the same consonant sound at the beginning of words that sit close together in a sentence.
Using a mild, indirect expression to replace a harsh, blunt, or unpleasant statement.
Placing two opposing ideas together in parallel structures to create a clear contrast.
Directly addressing an absent person, an abstract idea, or an inanimate object as if it were present and alive.
Arranging words, phrases, or clauses in an ascending order of importance or emotional weight.
A sudden drop from a dignified, important tone to a trivial or disappointing one.
A play on words that exploits multiple meanings or words that sound alike but mean different things.
An extended narrative metaphor where characters and events symbolize deeper moral or political truths.

topics.title: Contextual Cloze Text & Vocabulary Cohesion
topics.summary: This topic covers the Cloze Test, where you fill blanks in a passage by using meaning, grammar, natural word pairings (collocations) and linking words.
topics.exam_tip: When the options look the same, check the word right after the blank. If the next word is 'on' and the options are depend, rely, hinge or agree, study the context closely. A door hinges on a pivot, while people rely on friends.
topics.analogy: A Cloze Test is like a jigsaw puzzle with missing pieces. You cannot find the missing piece by staring only at the empty space. You must study the colours, shapes and patterns around it to find the word that fits perfectly.

sub_topics.title: How the Cloze Test Works
sub_topics.note: The Cloze Test is a passage of about 200 words with 10 blank spaces. It tests your vocabulary, sentence structure and reading flow. Unlike single vocabulary questions, you must understand how the whole sentence flows. Success depends on two things: collocation (natural word pairings like commit a crime or wreak havoc) and structural connectives (prepositions and conjunctions that link ideas).
sub_topics.formula: Correct Cloze Entry = Contextual Synonym + Syntactic Accordance + Collocational Match

sub_topics.title: Collocations and Prepositional Anchors
sub_topics.note: You cannot solve a blank on its own. Read the sentences before and after it to understand the theme and style. A preposition right after the blank can tell you which verb must come before it.
sub_topics.formula: Collocation Anchor = Verb + Mandated Preposition, e.g. abstain + from

flashcards.back: Filling blanks in a passage by evaluating sentence syntax, context, and structural vocabulary cohesion.
Words that naturally and frequently pair together in standard English usage.
The grammatical and lexical links that hold a text together and give it structural unity.
Vocabulary and technical terms specific to a particular field, profession, or subject area.
Words near a blank space that point to the meaning or grammatical form of the missing word.
Ensuring a chosen word matches the exact grammatical structure required by the sentence.
Conjunctions and prepositions that establish logical transitions between clauses.
Testing an option by inserting it into the blank to see if it preserves the meaning of the sentence.
Fixed word pairings that follow established idioms rather than standard literal rules.
Making sure a chosen word fits the overall theme and argument of the entire passage.
A preposition right after a blank that determines which verb can grammatically precede it.
Words like furthermore, consequently, or alternatively that signal the direction of the text's argument.
Pairs of words like either...or or not only...but also that dictate choices across a blank.
Eliminating options that repeat a meaning already expressed in the sentence.
Verifying if a blank requires a noun, verb, adjective, or adverb based on the sentence layout.
Ensuring options match nearby qualifiers like some, all, many, or few.
Singular or plural determiners (this, these, that, those) that limit the nouns that can fill a blank.
Maintaining a consistent timeline and perspective throughout the text.
Eliminating options that break standard punctuation or capitalization rules.
Keeping the core focus of the entire passage in mind when solving individual blank spaces.

topics.title: Prescribed Novel Characterization & Narrative Arc
topics.summary: This topic covers the set literature text, 'The Lekki Headmaster' by Kabir Alabi Garba: its characters, plot, settings and themes such as integrity, discipline and corruption.
topics.exam_tip: Pay close attention to scenes where the Headmaster confronts local corruption or handles pushback from the community. Questions often test the reasons behind these conflicts, not just the events.
topics.analogy: Studying the set novel is like analysing a chess match. You cannot just memorise where the pieces stand; you must understand why each player moves, trace their plans, and see how each move leads to the final checkmate.

sub_topics.title: Characters, Plot and Themes
sub_topics.note: JAMB sets specific questions on a chosen literature text, currently 'The Lekki Headmaster' by Kabir Alabi Garba. You are tested on character traits, key plot events, subplots, settings and central themes (such as integrity, discipline and systemic corruption). Look beyond simple plot summaries: understand why characters act as they do, trace how conflicts grow, and find the causes and effects of major turning points.
sub_topics.formula: Correct Character Option = Stated Motivation + Verified Action in Plot

sub_topics.title: Common Novel Traps
sub_topics.note: Distractors often mix up characters or give one character's words or actions to another. Always check who did or said what before choosing an answer.
sub_topics.formula: JAMB Trap = True Event + Swapped Character Actor

flashcards.back: Explicitly tracking characters, plot development, themes, and settings within the current set book.
Tracing the main character's development and challenges throughout the narrative.
The core idea, moral lesson, or social message exploring issues like integrity or reform.
The primary struggle between opposing forces (e.g., character vs. system) that drives the plot forward.
The character, institution, or social pressure that stands in direct opposition to the protagonist.
The physical locations, cultural environment, and time periods where the story takes place.
Secondary storylines that run alongside the main plot to add depth and support the core themes.
The underlying psychological reasons, values, or desires that drive a character's actions.
The highest point of tension or major turning point in the story's narrative arc.
The final stage of the story where conflicts are settled and character fates are determined.
Structural moments where the reader knows vital information that a character is unaware of.
An object, location, or repeating motif used to represent a larger abstract idea.
Tracking which character spoke specific lines during key turning points in the book.
Supporting characters designed to spark reactions or reveal key traits in the main characters.
A character whose traits contrast directly with another character to emphasize specific qualities.
Interrupting the timeline to show past events, filling in crucial backstory for characters.
Using a small setting, like a school, to represent and critique issues in the broader society.
Examining conversations to understand inner feelings, relationships, and hidden character agendas.
Situations where characters must make tough choices between conflicting moral values.
The writer's standpoint and social commentary, revealed through how characters are rewarded or punished.

sections.section_title: Section 2: Lexis, Structure and Grammatical Mechanics

topics.title: Subject-Verb Concord & Alternative Plurality
topics.summary: This topic covers how a verb must agree in number and person with its true subject, including tricky cases like either...or, as well as, many a and collective nouns.
topics.exam_tip: If you see Neither/Nor or Either/Or, ignore the first noun. Find the noun right next to the verb slot. If it is plural, choose a plural verb; if it is singular, choose a singular verb.
topics.analogy: Accompaniment concord is like a celebrity walking the red carpet with bodyguards. The cameras (the verb) focus only on the celebrity (Subject 1). The bodyguards (as well as, along with) are extras and do not change who gets the spotlight.

sub_topics.title: Proximity and Accompaniment Concord
sub_topics.note: Concord means the verb agrees with its true subject. With either...or, neither...nor and not only...but also, the verb matches the closest subject (proximity concord). Phrases like as well as, along with and together with are only extra information, so the verb matches the first subject and ignores the added one (accompaniment concord).
sub_topics.formula: Subject 1 + as well as / along with + Subject 2 -> Verb matches Subject 1 | Subject 1 + or / nor + Subject 2 -> Verb matches Subject 2

sub_topics.title: Many a and Collective Nouns
sub_topics.note: The modifier 'Many a' is singular: it always takes a singular noun and a singular verb. Collective nouns (like committee or team) take a singular verb when the group acts as one unit, and a plural verb when the members act individually or disagree.
sub_topics.formula: Many a + Singular Noun -> Singular Verb

breakdown: S - Singular for each and every
S - Split collective verbs for division

flashcards.back: The structural requirement that a verb must match its subject in both number and person.
Verb matches the nearest subject when clauses are linked by either...or, neither...nor, or, not only...but also.
Subject1 + (as well as / along with / together with) + Subject2 -> Verb matches Subject1 only.
Many a + Singular Noun -> Singular Verb.
Group nouns acting together as a single unit take a singular verb.
Group nouns whose members act individually or disagree take a plural verb.
Pronouns like everyone, someone, nobody, each, every are singular and take singular verbs.
One of + Plural Noun -> Singular Verb.
One of + Plural Noun + who/that relative clause -> Plural Verb.
A number of acts as a plural modifier and always takes a plural verb.
The number of points to a single fixed count and always takes a singular verb.
Nouns plural in spelling but singular in concept (physics, economics, news) take singular verbs.
Sums, equations, distances, amounts of money, and periods of time take singular verbs.
Nouns like scissors, spectacles, trousers take plural verbs unless preceded by 'a pair of'.
The verb matches the specific noun that follows the preposition 'of'.
Tracking the true subject when it is placed after the verb in sentences starting with there or here.
Modifiers like with, except, besides do not combine nouns into a plural compound subject.
More than one + Singular Noun -> Singular Verb.
Two distinct nouns joined by and take a plural verb unless they form a single combined concept (rice and beans).
Nothing but + Noun (singular or plural) -> Singular Verb.

topics.title: Tense Sequences, Aspect Matching & Time Markers
topics.summary: This topic covers keeping time order correct in compound and complex sentences, especially the Past Perfect, and matching tenses with time words like before, since and for.
topics.exam_tip: Look for the words 'before' or 'by the time' in past-tense sentences. If two past actions are described, find the one that happened first and make sure it uses had + past participle. Example: 'The train had left before we arrived.'
topics.analogy: Past Perfect is like a grandfather and Simple Past is like a father. Both belong to the past, but the grandfather (Past Perfect) is always older and comes before the father (Simple Past) in the family timeline.

sub_topics.title: Aspects and the Past Perfect
sub_topics.note: You must know the three aspects of verbs: Progressive (ongoing actions), Perfective (completed actions) and Habitual (repeated actions). JAMB often tests the Past Perfect (had + past participle), used to order two actions that both happened in the past. The action that finished first uses the Past Perfect; the later action uses the Simple Past.
sub_topics.formula: Action 1 (finished first) = Had + Past Participle | Action 2 (happened second) = Simple Past

sub_topics.title: Time Markers and Tense Consistency
sub_topics.note: Time words such as since, for, before and by the time decide which tense to use. If the main verb of a sentence is past, the verbs in the other clauses must also shift to a past form. Mixing up timelines or choosing the wrong helping verb is a common distractor trap.
sub_topics.formula: Sequence: Action 1 [Had + V3] -> before -> Action 2 [V2]

flashcards.back: The grammatical form of a verb that shows the time of an action (past, present, or future).
Shows how an action relates to time, focusing on whether it is complete, ongoing, or habitual.
Had + Past Participle; used for the earlier of two completed past actions.
Has/Have + Past Participle; links a past action directly to the present moment.
Will have + Past Participle; shows an action that will be completed before a specific future endpoint.
Expresses permanent facts, universal laws, or recurring routines.
If the principal verb of a sentence is past, subordinate clauses must shift to a past form as well.
Actions shown as in-progress at a specific point in time using a form of be + present participle.
Verbs of thought, emotion, or ownership (know, love, belong) cannot be used in continuous tenses.
Present Perfect Clause + since + Simple Past Clause.
Using the present tense to make past historical events feel vivid and immediate.
For shows a total duration of time; Since points to a specific starting moment.
Verbs that change vowels to form the past tense (sing/sang/sung) instead of adding -ed.
A verb form that focuses on the ongoing, incomplete nature of an action.
A verb form that views an action as a single, fully completed event.
Connection words like when, while, before, after, until that determine tense alignment.
Sudden, short actions that interrupt ongoing background activities, using the Simple Past.
Long-lasting background actions that use continuous verb forms.
Scientific or geographical facts stay in the present tense even inside past narratives.
Mixing up the past tense form (V2) with the past participle form (V3) without an auxiliary verb.

topics.title: Mood Shifts: Mandative Subjunctives & Unreal Passages
topics.summary: This topic covers the subjunctive mood, used for wishes, imaginary situations and urgent demands, including the 'It is high time' pattern.
topics.exam_tip: If a sentence begins 'It is high time we...', look only for options in the Simple Past. 'It is high time we studied' is correct, while 'It is high time we start studying' is an intentional trap.
topics.analogy: The subjunctive mood is like entering a courtroom. The moment you cross the door ('I demand that...'), normal street grammar is suspended. Verbs must take off their decorations (-s, -ed) and stand in their bare base form before the judge.

sub_topics.title: The Mandative Subjunctive
sub_topics.note: The mandative subjunctive is triggered by verbs of demand, advice or urgency (insist, demand, suggest, recommend) followed by a that-clause. It needs the base form of the verb: no -s ending and no -ed ending. Example: I suggest that he go.
sub_topics.formula: Demand Verb (insist / demand) + that + Subject -> Base Verb Form (no -s / -ed / -ing)

sub_topics.title: The Unreal Past Subjunctive
sub_topics.note: The unreal past is triggered by wish, as if, as though and it is high time. 'It is high time we...' needs the Simple Past to show an action is overdue. If no subject follows, use an infinitive phrase (it is time to go).
sub_topics.formula: It is high time + Subject -> Simple Past | It is high time + (no subject) -> To + Base Verb

breakdown: A - Alter with past for wishes

flashcards.back: Shows the speaker's attitude toward what they are saying, treating it as a fact, command, wish, or uncertainty.
Used for hypothetical situations, strong wishes, demands of urgency, or statements contrary to fact.
Command Verb + that + Subject + Base Verb (e.g., I suggest that he go).
It is high time + Subject + Simple Past Verb (shows an action is overdue).
It is high time + to + Base Verb.
Subject1 + would rather + Subject2 + Simple Past Verb (e.g., I'd rather you left).
Subject + would rather + Base Verb (when no second subject is introduced).
Using were for all subjects, including singular pronouns, to show an impossible condition.
Main Clause + as if + Subject + Past Subjunctive (shows a false present appearance).
Past Clause + as if + Subject + Past Perfect (shows a false past appearance).
Clauses starting with if, lest, or should that express possibilities or warnings.
Lest means 'for fear that' and must only pair with the base verb or the helper should.
The root, uninflected form of a verb with no tense markers or plural suffixes.
Expressions of blessings, wishes, or curses that use the base verb form (e.g., Long live the King).
Fixed, traditional expressions that keep old subjunctive rules alive (e.g., be that as it may).
Indicative states real facts; Subjunctive explores ideas, desires, or conditions contrary to fact.
Words like essential, vital, crucial, imperative that trigger the mandative subjunctive.
Using past subjunctive forms within the condition clause of Type 2 patterns.
Subject + wish + Subject + Simple Past Verb (shows discontent with current reality).
Using the subjunctive mood to express a deliberate choice, exercise of will, or formal request.

topics.title: Structural Conditionals: Hypotheses & Regrets
topics.summary: This topic covers the three main types of if-sentences (real, unreal and impossible past), plus inverted forms like 'Had I known...'.
topics.exam_tip: If a question starts 'Had I been told...', do not look for present tense options. This is an inverted Type 3 conditional. Look only for choices with 'would have' or 'could have' + past participle.
topics.analogy: The three conditional types are like a video game. Type 1 is a level you can easily win now. Type 2 is a fantasy level you are unlikely to enter. Type 3 is a level you already lost yesterday; you can only look back and wish you had played differently.

sub_topics.title: Type 1, Type 2 and Type 3 Conditionals
sub_topics.note: A conditional sentence has an if-clause (the condition) and a main clause (the result). Type 1 (real present or future): If + present -> will + base verb. Type 2 (unreal or unlikely present): If + past -> would + base verb. Type 3 (impossible past regret): If + past perfect -> would have + past participle.
sub_topics.formula: Type 1: If + Simple Present -> Will + Base | Type 2: If + Simple Past -> Would + Base | Type 3: If + Had + V3 -> Would Have + V3

sub_topics.title: Inverted Conditionals
sub_topics.note: JAMB often removes the word 'If' in Type 3 and moves 'Had' to the front of the sentence. The meaning stays the same: 'Had I known, I would have come' means 'If I had known, I would have come'.
sub_topics.formula: Inverted Type 3: Had + Subject + Past Participle -> Would Have + Past Participle

flashcards.back: A structure featuring an if-clause (condition) and a main clause (consequence) showing dependency.
If + Simple Present -> Will + Base Verb (shows a real future possibility).
If + Simple Past -> Would + Base Verb (shows an unreal or unlikely present scenario).
If + Past Perfect -> Would Have + Past Participle (shows an impossible past regret).
Had + Subject + Past Participle -> Would Have + Past Participle (drops the word if).
If + Simple Present -> Simple Present (used for scientific laws and absolute certainties).
If + Past Perfect -> Would + Base Verb (links a past condition to a present result).
If + Simple Past -> Would Have + Past Participle (links a continuous condition to a past result).
Means 'if not'; it introduces a negative condition and avoids double negatives in its clause.
Acts as an exact structural equivalent to if, introducing a mandatory requirement.
Were + Subject + Infinitive -> Would + Base Verb (e.g., Were I to jump...).
The outcome in a conditional structure that relies entirely on the if-clause happening.
Means 'if it hadn't been for'; always triggers a Type 3 conditional outcome.
Ensuring the core verb in a Type 3 outcome uses its third inflection form (V3).
Swapping would with could (ability) or might (possibility) to change the meaning of the outcome.
In case shows preparation for a potential event; If shows an action that happens only after a condition is met.
Imagining alternative outcomes to past events, which forms the basis of Type 3 structures.
If the if-clause comes first, add a comma; if the main clause comes first, remove the comma.
Should + Subject + Base Verb -> Will + Base Verb (adds a formal tone to a Type 1 condition).
A scenario in a Type 1 structure where the outcome remains completely unresolved but highly possible.

topics.title: Pronoun Case Assignment & Antecedent Alignment
topics.summary: This topic covers choosing the right pronoun form (I/me, who/whom) and making pronouns match the nouns they stand for in gender, number and person.
topics.exam_tip: Whenever a pronoun follows the word 'between', cross out options with I, he, she or they. Prepositions must be followed by the objective case. 'Between you and me' is correct; 'Between you and I' is an intentional trap.
topics.analogy: Pronouns are like actors in costumes. The Subjective costume (I, he, she) is worn only by actors performing actions at the front of the stage. The Objective costume (me, him, her) is worn by those receiving actions or standing behind the preposition gate. Putting 'I' after a preposition is like an actor wearing the wrong costume.

sub_topics.title: Subjective, Objective and Possessive Case
sub_topics.note: Pronouns must match their antecedents in gender, number and person, and their position decides their case. Subjective case (I, we, he, she, they, who) is used when the pronoun does the action. Objective case (me, us, him, her, them, whom) is used when the pronoun receives the action or follows a preposition. Possessive case: my, mine, our, ours, his, her, hers, their, theirs, its.
sub_topics.formula: Preposition (Between / For / To) + Pronoun -> Objective Case [me / him / her / them]

sub_topics.title: Comparisons and Who vs Whom
sub_topics.note: JAMB sets traps with 'than' and 'as' (he is taller than I, not me) and with prepositions (between you and me, not between you and I). Use 'who' when the pronoun is the subject of the verb and 'whom' when it is the object.
sub_topics.formula: Than / As + Pronoun -> Subjective Case [I / he / she / they] + (implied verb) | Who = subject, Whom = object

flashcards.back: The form a pronoun takes based on its grammatical role as a subject, object, or possessor.
Pronoun forms (I, we, he, she, they, who) used as the subject of a verb.
Pronoun forms (me, us, him, her, them, whom) used as direct/indirect objects or after prepositions.
Forms like mine, ours, his, hers, theirs that show ownership independently without following a noun.
The original noun or noun phrase that a pronoun refers back to and replaces.
Preposition + Pronoun1 + and + Pronoun2 -> Both pronouns must be in the objective case (between you and me).
Subject + Verb + Adjective-er + than + Subjective Pronoun (e.g., He runs faster than I).
Pronouns ending in -self or -selves; they cannot be used as subjects without an accompanying noun or pronoun.
Use who if the pronoun acts as the subject of the following verb (replaceable by he/they).
Use whom if the pronoun acts as the object of a verb or preposition (replaceable by him/them).
Words like someone, anyone, everyone require singular pronouns for agreement in formal syntax.
Selecting who, whom, whose, or which based on its structural role inside a relative clause.
Keeping pronoun cases consistent when linking them across coordinate conjunctions.
Its (no apostrophe) is possessive; It's (with apostrophe) is a contraction for it is or it has.
Matching this/that with singular nouns and these/those with plural nouns.
Each other (used for two people) and one another (used for three or more people).
If a sentence starts with the generic subject one, it must use one's or one throughout the sentence.
Avoiding sudden shifts between first person (I), second person (you), and third person (he/she/they).
Shifting pronouns to the objective case when they modify an object noun in apposition (e.g., He scolded us, the students).
A noun or pronoun modifying a gerund (-ing noun) must be in the possessive case (e.g., I dislike his coming late).

topics.title: Adjective Order (OSASCOMP) & Modifier Pitfalls
topics.summary: This topic covers the fixed order of adjectives before a noun (OSASCOMP) and common modifier mistakes like double comparatives and dangling modifiers.
topics.exam_tip: Write OSASCOMP on your scratch paper as soon as the exam starts. For adjective order questions, do not read the options aloud to see how they sound. Check the adjectives against the letters of the formula to find the correct order.
topics.analogy: Adjective order is like an airport boarding queue. No matter how creative an adjective is, it must stand in its assigned position. Opinion adjectives board first, while Material and Purpose adjectives board last, right next to the noun.

sub_topics.title: The OSASCOMP Order
sub_topics.note: When several adjectives describe one noun, they follow this order: 1. Opinion (beautiful, ugly), 2. Size (large, tiny), 3. Age (old, modern), 4. Shape (round, square), 5. Colour (black, reddish), 6. Origin (Nigerian, British), 7. Material (wooden, metallic), 8. Purpose (cooking, sewing). JAMB gives options with scrambled orders.
sub_topics.formula: Opinion -> Size -> Age -> Shape -> Colour -> Origin -> Material -> Purpose -> Noun

sub_topics.title: Modifier Pitfalls
sub_topics.note: Avoid double comparatives (more taller is wrong; say taller). Fix dangling modifiers, where an opening descriptive phrase is not attached to its true subject. Example fix: 'Walking home, I saw a snake' instead of 'Walking home, a snake was seen'.
sub_topics.formula: Dangling Modifier Fix: Opening Phrase (Action) + comma + True Subject Doing That Action

flashcards.back: The mandatory grammatical sequence used when multiple descriptive modifiers precede a noun.
Subjective judgments (charming, horrible) always occupy the first slot in the sequence.
Physical dimensions (mammoth, microscopic) occupy the second slot in the sequence.
Temporal status (antique, contemporary) occupies the third slot in the sequence.
Geometric forms (cylindrical, spherical) occupy the fourth slot in the sequence.
Visual hues (crimson, translucent) occupy the fifth slot in the sequence.
Geographic or cultural source (Ghanaian, European) occupies the sixth slot in the sequence.
The physical substance an object is made of (plastic, woolen) occupies the seventh slot, sitting close to the noun.
The designated function of an item (dining, tracking) occupies the final slot right before the noun.
A descriptive opening phrase that accidentally modifies the wrong noun due to incorrect sentence layout.
A modifier placed too far from the word it describes, making the sentence ambiguous or confusing.
A grammatical error caused by pairing the modifier more with an adjective that already ends in -er (e.g., more faster).
Adjectives like unique, dead, perfect that cannot be graded or compared using more or most.
Correctly positioning adverbs of frequency, manner, and place so they don't break up cohesive verb phrases.
Modifying an adjective to compare two entities, using either an -er suffix or the word more.
Modifying an adjective to compare three or more entities, using either an -est suffix or the word most.
Adjectives describing qualities that can exist in different intensities, allowing them to pair with modifiers like very.
Multi-word modifiers joined by hyphens when they appear before a noun (e.g., a well-known author).
Adjectives placed after a linking verb that modify the subject without sitting directly before it.
Verb forms ending in -ed or -ing that function structurally as descriptive adjectives.

topics.title: Prepositional Monopolies & Phrasal Collocations
topics.summary: This topic covers verbs, adjectives and idioms that must go with one particular preposition, and phrasal verbs whose meaning changes with the preposition.
topics.exam_tip: Watch the word 'prefer'. JAMB tempts you with 'than' (I prefer tea than coffee). The rule is absolute: prefer pairs only with 'to' (I prefer tea to coffee). The same applies to adjectives ending in -ior, such as superior to and inferior to.
topics.analogy: Prepositional monopolies are like arranged marriages in grammar. The verb and its preposition are bound together by convention. No matter how much another preposition seems to fit, you cannot break up the pair.

sub_topics.title: Fixed Verb and Preposition Pairs
sub_topics.note: Some verbs, adjectives and idioms must pair with one specific preposition. In formal British English you congratulate someone ON an achievement (never for), you are good AT an activity (not in), and you comply WITH a directive (not to). JAMB also tests wrong prepositions that come from local speech patterns.
sub_topics.formula: Congratulate -> on | Prefer -> to | Abstain -> from | Comply -> with | Adhere -> to

sub_topics.title: Phrasal Verbs
sub_topics.note: Phrasal verbs change meaning completely depending on the word attached to the verb, for example break down, break up and break off all mean different things. Always check the meaning of the full phrase, not just the root verb.
sub_topics.formula: Base Verb + Mandated Preposition Partner = Grammatical Collocation

flashcards.back: Fixed structural pairings where a specific noun, verb, or adjective commands one particular preposition.
Must always pair with the preposition on (e.g., I congratulate you on your graduation).
Must always pair with the preposition to when comparing choices (never use than).
Must always pair with the preposition from (e.g., abstain from voting).
An idiomatic phrase combining a verb with a preposition or adverb to create a brand-new meaning.
Must always pair with the preposition with (never use to).
Must always pair with the preposition to (e.g., adhere to regulations).
Adjectives like superior, inferior, senior, junior require the preposition to instead of than.
Must always pair with the preposition of (e.g., accused of theft; never use for).
You either blame something on someone, or you blame someone for something.
Selecting at for precise points and in for enclosed geographic boundaries or areas.
Selecting at for precise hours, on for specific days/dates, and in for months/years.
You are angry with a person, but angry at an action, object, or situation.
A person is familiar with a topic, but a topic is familiar to a person.
Must always pair with the preposition into (e.g., incorporated into the system).
Standard syntax accepts ending relative clauses with prepositions (e.g., the house he lived in).
Must always pair with the preposition of (e.g., deprived of his rights).
Must always pair with the preposition to (e.g., immune to the disease).
Idiom meaning to lose emotional control, or for a mechanical vehicle to stop working.
Idiom meaning to cause an event to happen or to introduce a change.

topics.title: Lexical Registers: Technical Vocabulary Domains
topics.summary: This topic covers words that belong to particular fields such as law, medicine, business, politics, media, science and farming, and choosing the exact technical term for the topic.
topics.exam_tip: If a Cloze passage is about business or banking and the blank describes money paid to shareholders, options like profit, gain or allocation are distractors. Pick the exact financial term: dividend.
topics.analogy: Lexical registers are like uniforms for different professions. A doctor does not wear a judge's wig to surgery, and a lawyer does not carry a stethoscope to court. Your word choice must wear the uniform the passage's topic demands.

sub_topics.title: The Seven Registers
sub_topics.note: JAMB tests words that belong to particular fields. The seven main registers are: 1. Legal (plaintiff, defendant, subpoena, litigation, affidavit). 2. Medical (prognosis, diagnosis, acute, chronic, outpatient). 3. Commercial/Financial (dividend, liabilities, asset, inflation, revenue). 4. Political/Administrative (franchise, bureaucracy, constituency, incumbent). 5. Journalism/Media (editorial, censorship, libel, syndication). 6. Scientific/Technological (hypothesis, empirical, systemic, syntax). 7. Agricultural (silage, arable, fallow, husbandry, pastoral).
sub_topics.formula: Passage Subject (e.g. Court Case) -> Filter Options -> Choose the Strict Legal Register Term

sub_topics.title: Technical Term vs Generic Word
sub_topics.note: In Cloze tests and lexis questions, general descriptions are wrong. You must choose the specific technical word that fits the field. For example, pick 'verdict' instead of the general word 'decision' in a court passage.
sub_topics.formula: Generic Word Trap is not equal to Technical Register Term

flashcards.back: A specialized variety of vocabulary and phrasing used within a specific profession, science, or social domain.
The party or individual who initiates a lawsuit against a defendant in a court of law.
A formal, legally binding written order commanding a witness to appear and testify in court.
A medical doctor's professional forecast or prediction regarding the likely course and outcome of a disease.
A medical condition or illness that persists over a long duration and is difficult to cure completely.
A portion of a corporation's earnings distributed directly to its shareholders based on ownership.
The financial debts, obligations, or legal responsibilities owed by a business entity to outside parties.
The constitutional right or privilege granted to citizens to cast their votes in public elections.
The official who currently holds an elected political office during an active election cycle.
A false, malicious published written statement that damages a person's reputation.
An opinion article written by the senior staff or editor of a newspaper reflecting its official stance.
Information, verification, or knowledge derived directly from systematic observation or experiment.
Land that is naturally suitable or cleared for plowing and cultivating crops.
Cultivated land that is deliberately left unseeded for a season to regenerate its soil nutrients.
A formal, written statement of facts confirmed by the oath of the party making it before a legal authority.
A medical condition or symptom that begins suddenly, is severe, but lasts for a short duration.
Valuable items, property, or resources owned by an individual or corporation that hold economic worth.
A complex administrative system marked by rigid hierarchies, fixed procedures, and red tape.
Green forage or fodder that is preserved through fermentation inside a silo to feed livestock during winter or dry seasons.
Licensing and selling media content, articles, or broadcasts to multiple independent media outlets simultaneously.

topics.title: Idioms, Synonyms & Antonyms in Context
topics.summary: This topic covers working out the meaning of words and idioms from the sentence they are in, and finding words with the same or opposite meaning.
topics.exam_tip: If an idiom question asks about 'to kick the bucket' or 'to smell a rat', cross out choices about actual buckets, water, rodents or smells. The correct answer is always the figurative meaning (death, or suspecting trickery).
topics.analogy: Words are like chameleons: they change colour based on the branch they sit on. 'Draw' means sketch in an art class, pull out a weapon in a cowboy standoff, and a tied score at a football match. Never judge a word until you check its background.

sub_topics.title: Context Decides Meaning
sub_topics.note: JAMB tests your ability to interpret words and phrases in context. An underlined word may have a common dictionary meaning, but the sentence can change that meaning completely. Context overrides the general definition.
sub_topics.formula: Correct Contextual Option = Substitution Check Passes Without Changing Sentence Tone or Grammar

sub_topics.title: Idiomatic Expressions
sub_topics.note: An idiom cannot be understood from the literal meaning of its words. JAMB often puts a very literal meaning as bait, usually in Option A or B, to catch unprepared students. Choose the figurative explanation.
sub_topics.formula: Idiomatic Expression is not equal to the Literal Sum of Its Words

breakdown: A - Avoid literal traps in idioms
P - Pinpoint matching parts of speech

flashcards.back: Choosing synonyms or antonyms based entirely on how a word functions inside a specific sentence.
A fixed group of words carrying a figurative meaning that cannot be deduced from the literal definitions of the individual words.
An idiomatic expression meaning to settle an argument, forgive a grudge, and make peace.
An idiomatic expression meaning to reveal a secret prematurely or indiscreetly.
Words like fleeting, ephemeral, temporary that show something lasts for only a brief moment.
Words like permanent, enduring, perpetual showing something lasts indefinitely.
An idiom meaning to view a statement with skepticism and not accept it as absolute truth.
An idiomatic expression meaning to work, study, or read late into the night.
Words that share the same spelling or sound but carry entirely different meanings (bank of a river vs. money bank).
Replacing an underlined idiomatic phrase with a single concise word that preserves the message.
An idiomatic expression meaning to stop working on an activity for the rest of the daytime.
An idiomatic expression meaning to stay loyal through all challenges, hardships, and good times.
Words like alleviate, ease, lessen, assuage that mean to reduce the severity of something.
Words like aggravate, exacerbate, intensify that mean to make a situation worse.
An unpredictable factor, individual, or element that can completely alter an outcome.
An idiomatic expression meaning an event happened at the last possible moment or right before a deadline.
Words like showy, pretentious, gaudy, flamboyant that describe displaying wealth or status boastfully.
Words like modest, humble, understated, reserved that describe a quiet, simple style.
An idiom meaning to speak indirectly and avoid addressing the core issue directly.
An idiomatic expression for a misfortune that ultimately yields positive, beneficial results later on.

sections.section_title: Section 3: Mechanics, Voice Transformations and Clauses

topics.title: Capitalization, Spelling Rules & Punctuation Mechanics
topics.summary: This topic covers apostrophes for possession, British versus American spelling, tricky spellings, and the difference between the semicolon and the colon.
topics.exam_tip: 'Its' vs 'It's' is a guaranteed JAMB question. It's means 'it is' or 'it has'. Its shows possession. 'The dog wagged it's tail' is wrong; it must be 'its tail'. Possessive pronouns (ours, yours, theirs, its) never take an apostrophe. Also learn the double-letter words: Accommodation (two c, two m), Embarrassment (two r, two s), Harassment, Millennium, Committee.
topics.analogy: A semicolon is like a drop of heavy-duty superglue. It is stronger than a comma, which would cause a comma splice if used alone. The semicolon can fuse two full sentences together without needing and, but or because.

sub_topics.title: The Possession Apostrophe
sub_topics.note: Singular nouns, and plural nouns not ending in -s, take 's (the child's book, the women's clinic). Plural nouns ending in -s take only a trailing apostrophe (the boys' hostel). For singular names ending in an s sound (Jesus, Moses), British English accepts either Jesus' disciples or Jesus's disciples, but JAMB prefers the trailing apostrophe for classical and historical names.
sub_topics.formula: Singular + 's | Plural ending in -s + ' | Irregular plural (not ending in -s) + 's

sub_topics.title: British vs American Spelling
sub_topics.note: JAMB tests British English (UK) only, and American spellings are marked wrong. UK: Honour, Colour, Centre, Theatre, Programme, Dialogue, Travelling, Enrolment, Defence. US: Honor, Color, Center, Theater, Program, Dialog, Traveling, Enrollment, Defense.
sub_topics.formula: UK: -our, -re, double l (travelled) | US: -or, -er, single l (traveled)

sub_topics.title: Semicolon vs Colon
sub_topics.note: A semicolon joins two closely related independent clauses without a joining word (The rain started; we ran inside). A colon introduces a list, an explanation or a direct quote after an independent clause (He bought three items: a book, a pen, and a bag).
sub_topics.formula: Independent Clause ; Independent Clause | Independent Clause : List / Explanation / Quote

mnemonics.meaning: I before E, except after C
breakdown: Use I before E: believe, relief
Except right after C: receive, deceive, ceiling
Or when it sounds like A: neighbour, weigh
Compliment with an I is something I like to hear (praise)
Complement with an E completes a set or extends something

flashcards.back: Singular Noun + 's (even if it ends in s, add 's for modern names). Example: James's car / The girl's book.
Plural Noun ending in -s + ' (apostrophe only). Example: The students' union / The teachers' lounge.
Plural Noun not ending in -s + 's. Example: The children's playground / The women's wing.
It's = It is / It has | Its = Possessive (no apostrophe). Example: The bird hurt its wing (not it's).
Must feature a double C and a double M: A-C-C-O-M-M-O-D-A-T-I-O-N.
Must feature a double R and a double S: E-M-B-A-R-R-A-S-S-M-E-N-T.
Features a single R but a double S: H-A-R-A-S-S-M-E-N-T (never double the R).
Connects two independent clauses without a coordinating conjunction. Example: He went to Lagos; she stayed in Ibadan.
Independent Clause + : + List, Explanation, or Quote. Example: She ordered three fruits: apples, oranges, and grapes.
UK uses -our | US uses -or (JAMB strictly marks -our as correct). Examples: Labour, Behaviour, Vigour, Humour.
UK uses -re | US uses -er (JAMB strictly marks -re as correct). Examples: Centre, Theatre, Metre, Calibre.
Verbs ending in a single 'l' double it when adding suffixes starting with vowels in UK English. Examples: Travel -> Travelled, Travelling; Cancel -> Cancelled.
Stationery (with an 'e') = paper and pens | Stationary (with an 'a') = not moving. Example: He bought books at the stationery store. The car remained stationary.
Joining two independent clauses with only a comma is grammatically incorrect. 'I am tired, I want to sleep' is wrong; 'I am tired; I want to sleep' is correct.
Use a hyphen when two or more words act as a single adjective before a noun. Example: A well-known headmaster (but: The headmaster is well known).
Must feature a double L and a double N: M-I-L-L-E-N-N-I-U-M.
Adjectives derived from proper nouns must always be capitalized. Examples: The Nigerian economy, Shakespearean sonnets.
Under British style (traditional JAMB standard), punctuation sits outside quotation marks unless it belongs to the quote. Example: He described the exam as "very easy".
Derived from maintain, but the spelling changes: M-A-I-N-T-E-N-A-N-C-E (not maintainance).
Features an 'a' in the middle, not an 'e': S-E-P-A-R-A-T-I-O-N (not seperated).

topics.title: Voice Transformations & Rhetorical Structures
topics.summary: This topic covers changing sentences from active to passive voice and from direct speech to reported (indirect) speech without changing the meaning.
topics.exam_tip: In reported speech, watch for options that wrongly keep the word 'tomorrow'. Example: 'I will clear my desk tomorrow,' said John becomes: John said that he would clear his desk the next day. Also, when an active question starts with Who, the passive must start with 'By whom'.
topics.analogy: Reported speech is like being a news reporter describing an event from last week. You cannot use current time words. If the politician said 'I am building a road here today', you tell your audience that he said he was building a road there that day.

sub_topics.title: Active and Passive Voice
sub_topics.note: In the active voice the subject performs the action (The boy killed the rat). In the passive voice the object becomes the subject, with a form of 'to be' + past participle (The rat was killed by the boy). Intransitive verbs (arrive, sleep, die) take no object, so they cannot be made passive. A 'Who' question becomes 'By whom' in the passive: Who broke the window? -> By whom was the window broken?
sub_topics.formula: Subject + Verb + Object -> Object + [Be Verb] + Past Participle + [by Subject]

sub_topics.title: Direct to Indirect Speech
sub_topics.note: After a past tense reporting verb (He said...), three things change. Tense backshift: Simple Present -> Simple Past; Present Perfect or Simple Past -> Past Perfect; Will -> Would. Pronoun shift: I -> he/she; we -> they. Time and place words: here -> there; now -> then; tomorrow -> the next day; yesterday -> the previous day.
sub_topics.formula: Can -> Could | May -> Might | Will -> Would | Must -> Had to | Now -> Then | Today -> That day | Have -> Had

breakdown: Take one giant step backward in time when reporting someone's words
Today steps back to That day

flashcards.back: Subject + Verb + Object -> Object + [Be Verb Form] + Past Participle + [by Subject]. Example: The dog bit the man -> The man was bitten by the dog.
Who + Active Verb...? -> By whom + Auxiliary Verb + Object + Past Participle? Example: Who wrote the poem? -> By whom was the poem written?
Direct Simple Present -> Indirect Simple Past. Example: 'I love football,' he said -> He said that he loved football.
Direct Present Perfect -> Indirect Past Perfect. Example: 'I have finished,' she said -> She said that she had finished.
Direct Simple Past -> Indirect Past Perfect (a JAMB favourite). Example: 'I bought a book yesterday,' he said -> He said he had bought a book the previous day.
Direct: Tomorrow -> Indirect: The next day or The following day. Example: 'We will leave tomorrow' -> They said they would leave the next day.
Direct: Yesterday -> Indirect: The previous day or The day before. Example: 'I ran yesterday' -> He said he had run the previous day.
Can -> Could | May -> Might | Will -> Would | Must -> Had to. Example: 'You must go' -> He told me that I had to go.
Intransitive verbs cannot take a passive form because they lack objects. Example: 'He died peacefully' cannot be made passive.
Indirect wh- questions keep the question word but drop the inversion (subject before verb, no do/did). Example: 'Where do you live?' -> He asked me where I lived (not where did I live).
Add if or whether before the clause. Example: 'Are you coming?' -> He asked whether I was coming.
If the direct statement is an ongoing universal truth, do not shift the tense backward. Example: 'The sun is hot,' he said -> He said that the sun is (not was) hot.
Either the direct object or the indirect object can become the new passive subject. Example: He gave me a pen -> A pen was given to me OR I was given a pen.
Reporting Verb (ordered/told) + Object + Infinitive Phrase (to + verb). Example: 'Sit down!' -> The teacher ordered the students to sit down.
Change 'Don't + Verb' to 'not to + verb'. Example: 'Don't touch it,' he said -> He warned me not to touch it.
Used when the agent performing the action is unknown or obvious. Example: The thief was arrested (by the police is understood).

flashcards.front: Say vs. Tell in Reported Speech
flashcards.back: Tell must be followed immediately by a personal object; Say does not take a personal object directly unless using 'to'. Example: He told me that he was tired; He said that he was tired.
Direct Past Perfect sentences cannot shift further back; they remain past perfect. Example: 'I had left before they arrived' -> He said he had left before they arrived.
Suggest + that + Object + should be + Past Participle. Example: He suggested building a school -> He suggested that a school should be built.
Exclamatory sentences convert into clauses using words like exclaimed with joy/sorrow. Example: 'Alas! I failed,' he said -> He exclaimed sorrowfully that he had failed.

topics.title: Nominal, Adjectival & Adverbial Subordinate Clauses
topics.summary: This topic covers naming a phrase or clause and stating its job in the sentence: noun clauses, adjectival (relative) clauses and adverbial clauses of time, place, reason, condition, concession and more.
topics.exam_tip: JAMB wants a two-part answer: the grammatical name AND the function. For an adjectival clause, write 'It modifies the noun [name]'. For a nominal clause that is an object, write 'It is the object of the verb [name]'. Also, Although/Even though clauses are Concession (contrast), not Reason, even if 'Reason' is placed in Option A as bait.
topics.analogy: A sentence is like a theatre production, and nouns, adjectives and adverbs are actors. When one actor is tired, a whole group of words holding hands (a clause) steps onto the stage to play that role. In the noun's place, they act as a Noun Clause. Following a noun to describe it, they act as an Adjective Clause.

sub_topics.title: Phrase vs Clause, and Nominal Clauses
sub_topics.note: A phrase is a group of words without a finite verb (in the morning). A clause has a subject and a finite verb (when the morning came). Nominal (noun) clauses work as nouns. They can be the subject of a verb ([What he said] surprised us) or the object of a verb (I know [that he is honest]).
sub_topics.formula: Noun Clause Test: replace the clause with 'it'. If the sentence still makes sense, it is a Nominal Clause.

sub_topics.title: Adjectival (Relative) Clauses
sub_topics.note: Adjectival clauses modify a noun or pronoun that comes before them. They almost always begin with who, which, whose, that or whom. Example: The boy [who stole the money] has been caught. The clause modifies the noun 'boy'.
sub_topics.formula: Noun + [Relative Pronoun Clause] -> modifies the noun directly to its left

sub_topics.title: Adverbial Clauses
sub_topics.note: Adverbial clauses modify verbs, adjectives or adverbs, telling when, where, why, how or under what condition something happened. Time: He left [when the bell rang]. Concession: She passed [although she didn't study hard].
sub_topics.formula: Time: when, while, before, after | Concession: although, though | Condition: if, unless | Reason: because, since, as | Place: where | Manner: as if | Purpose: so that, lest | Result: so...that | Comparison: than

breakdown: If you can replace the whole underlined clause with IT or THAT and the sentence still makes sense
Then it is a Nominal (Noun) Clause
An adjectival clause acts like an arrow
The relative pronoun (who/which) points directly to the noun sitting immediately to its left

flashcards.back: [What/That Clause] + Main Verb + Extension. Example: What he did annoyed the teacher. (Noun Clause | Subject of the verb annoyed).
Subject + Transitive Verb + [What/That Clause]. Example: She believes that you are innocent. (Noun Clause | Object of the verb believes).
Noun + [Relative Pronoun Clause]. Example: The lady who spoke to us is our principal. (Adjectival Clause | Modifies the noun lady).
Clause introduced by when, while, before, after, as soon as. Example: We stood up when the governor walked in. (Adverbial Clause of Time | Modifies the verb stood up).
Clause introducing a contrast via although, even though, though, whereas. Example: He failed although he studied hard. (Adverbial Clause of Concession | Modifies the verb failed).
Clause introducing a dependency via if, unless, provided that. Example: You will fail unless you study. (Adverbial Clause of Condition | Modifies the verb will fail).
Clause introduced by because, since, as. Example: He stayed home because he was ill. (Adverbial Clause of Reason | Modifies the verb stayed).
Phrase = no finite verb | Clause = contains a finite verb. Example: In the dark room (Phrase) vs. Because the room was dark (Clause).
Modifies an inanimate noun directly to its left. Example: The book which I bought is lost. (Adjectival Clause | Modifies the noun book).
Preposition + [Noun Clause]. Example: Pay close attention to what the instructor says. (Noun Clause | Object of the preposition to).
Clause introduced by where or wherever. Example: Put the key where you found it. (Adverbial Clause of Place | Modifies the verb put).
Clause introduced by as if, as though, as. Example: He ran as if a lion were chasing him. (Adverbial Clause of Manner | Modifies the verb ran).
Clause introduced by so that, in order that, lest. Example: Study hard so that you can score high. (Adverbial Clause of Purpose | Modifies the verb study).
Clause introduced by so...that or such...that. Example: He was so weak that he fainted. (Adverbial Clause of Result | Modifies the adjective weak).

flashcards.front: Noun Clause as Complement of Subject
flashcards.back: Subject + Linking Verb (is/was) + [Noun Clause]. Example: The truth is that he stole it. (Noun Clause | Complement of the subject truth).
JAMB will delete the word whom or that to hide an adjectival clause. Example: The man [I saw] is here (short for The man whom I saw). It still functions as an adjectival clause modifying man.
Replace the clause with 'it'. If valid, it is a Noun Clause. Example: [What he saw] was scary -> It was scary. (Confirmed: Noun Clause).
Introduced by than or as...as. Example: She sings better than her sister does. (Adverbial Clause of Comparison | Modifies the adverb better).
Explains or renames a noun directly preceding it, usually separated by commas. Example: The news, that the plane crashed, shocked everyone. (Noun Clause | In apposition to the noun news).
Lest means 'for fear that' and must be followed by a base verb or should (never use will/not). Example: Run fast lest you should miss the bus. (Adverbial Clause of Purpose | Modifies the verb run).
